Title: Sam Bankman-Fried Trial Opening Statements and First Witness
Summary: Prosecution and defense opening statements contrasted Bankman-Fried as a villain versus a good-faith founder, followed by the first prosecution witness testimony regarding failed withdrawals.

On the second day of the trial, prosecutors led by Thane Rehn opened with a 30-minute statement characterizing Sam Bankman-Fried as a 'man' who stole billions from thousands of victims. They alleged he built FTX on lies, using Alameda Research and Caroline Ellison as fronts for secret access to customer funds, forging documents, and lying to the world. The prosecution highlighted his lavish lifestyle, including international travel, celebrity associations, and political donations.

Defense attorney Mark Cohen countered that Bankman-Fried did not defraud anyone, portraying him as a 'nerdy startup founder' acting in 'good faith' rather than a 'cartoon of a villain.' Cohen noted that Bankman-Fried spent about seven weeks in a Brooklyn prison.

During the defense's opening, Bankman-Fried defended Alameda as a successful hedge fund and FTX as an innovative company, not a Ponzi scheme. He claimed Alameda operated legally as a customer, processor, and market maker, using the analogy that 'working at a startup is like building a plane as you're flying it.' He blamed Ellison for failing to protect the fund from market risks and stated he was willing to give up personal wealth to make customers whole, concluding, 'Sam started and built two billion-dollar businesses,' and 'He didn't steal any money.'

The first prosecution witness was Marc-Antoine Julliard, a Paris-born cocoa trader living in London. Julliard testified that he invested in FTX in 2021, trading Bitcoin and Dogecoin, and failed to withdraw almost $100,000 on November 8.

Title: Tech news: AI startups, Google Pixel 8, and corporate updates
Summary: Covers Induced AI's teen founders, Google's Pixel 8 hardware launch, Flexport's CEO ouster, SBF trial details, Gmail spam rules, LinkedIn AI tools, X post volume disputes, IronNet's collapse, Acurable's wearable tech, battery software, and AI investment trends.

Induced AI, founded this year by two teenagers, assists businesses in automating workflows by converting plain English back-office task instructions to pseudo-code in real time. Google's annual hardware event showcased the Pixel 8, Pixel 8 Pro, Pixel Fold, Android 14, Pixel Buds, Google Assistant, Bard, and Pixel Watch 2. The Pixel 8 Pro features improved cameras, a brighter screen, and enhanced AI-powered features compared to the Pixel 7 Pro, though it includes an underutilized temperature sensor. Dave Clark, former Amazon executive, was ousted as CEO of Flexport just a year into the job; he later criticized the company following a CNBC report on his last days at the $8 billion freight forwarding startup. Details from Michael Lewis's book 'Going Infinite' emerged during the Manhattan Federal Court trial of Sam Bankman-Fried, alleging he tried to buy off Trump to prevent him from running for president again. Jacquelyn and Alex reported on the SBF trial at the Southern District of New York courthouse, where Bankman-Fried faced charges of knowingly committing fraud for wealth and power. Gmail announced changes effective next year requiring bulk email senders to authenticate emails, provide an easy unsubscribe method, and stay under a reported spam threshold. LinkedIn launched AI tools for job hunting, marketing, and sales, including an updated Recruiter platform, an AI Learning coach, and a marketing campaign tool. Elon Musk stated X generated 100–200 million daily posts in September, while CEO Linda Yaccarino later claimed 500 million posts per day. IronNet, founded in 2014 by former NSA director Keith Alexander, collapsed after going public in August 2021, laying off staff and seeing its stock price decline despite raising over $400 million. Esther Rodriguez-Villegas, a career academic, founded Acurable to create wearable devices that diagnose and manage respiratory conditions like sleep apnea and epilepsy at home. Breathe Battery Technologies created software for lithium-ion batteries to enable faster charging speeds or greater longevity. Anna surveyed 10 investors regarding the future of AI, covering startup opportunities, oligopoly dynamics, first-mover advantages, and the value of proprietary data.
